title: How to Know If Your AI Agent Is Any Good: Evals With Phoenix & Claude — Laurie Voss, Arize AI
talk_summary: Laurie Voss (Arize) walks through a full eval loop for an LLM agent: auto-trace every step with OpenTelemetry/Phoenix, manually read traces to find failure categories, then write code evals, LLM-judge evals, and human golden labels, validate the judge against humans, run before/after experiments, and gate CI on the results. The core claim is that prompt/model changes without evals are just vibes, and that judges must themselves be tested like classifiers (precision/recall, bias, splits).

takeaways.technique: Trace-first error analysis before writing any eval
takeaways.what_they_do: Instrument the agent so every LLM call, tool call, and span is auto-traced (OpenTelemetry/OpenInference), then manually read ~12+ traces end-to-end and write open notes, then group into failure categories (axial coding) before writing evals.
takeaways.evidence_quote: If you automate before you understand how your agent fails, you're going to end up measuring what's easy to measure instead of what actually matters.
takeaways.numbers: Read 12-16 traces manually; coding agent did error analysis in ~9 minutes

takeaways.technique: Code evals for deterministic checks, LLM judge only for meaning
takeaways.what_they_do: Split evals: cheap deterministic functions (does output parse, contain the ticker, stay under length, DB/API state correct) run in milliseconds for free; LLM judges only for semantic questions like faithfulness/actionability. Warns against one 'god evaluator'.
takeaways.numbers: Code eval ran 'almost instantly' and found 2 failures out of 15

takeaways.technique: Validate the LLM judge against human golden labels (precision/recall)
takeaways.what_they_do: Treat the judge as a classifier: humans label a golden set with the same rubric, run the judge against it as an experiment, report agreement plus precision/recall, and split into dev/test sets so you don't tune on the test set. Prioritize recall (catch all defects) over precision.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Your judge is a classifier in the classic ML sense... you measure it by comparing its predictions with the truth.
takeaways.numbers: Judge agreed with human 12/12 on dev; a 'more specific' rubric change dropped it to 11/12 and broke a test example

takeaways.technique: Gate CI on eval scorecards with guardrail vs north-star thresholds
takeaways.what_they_do: Wrap evals in a normal test runner (Vitest), run the agent on a regression set, and gate the build on acceptance criteria: hard guardrails must pass, noisy LLM-judge metrics gate on an average threshold rather than a single run.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Mention sticker is a guardrail. It has to be talking about the right company... actionability is a target. The average has to stay 08 or better.
takeaways.numbers: CI suite ~4 minutes; gate on average >= 0.8 for noisy judge metric

takeaways.technique: Use evals to decide model swaps and judge with a different/stronger model
takeaways.what_they_do: Run the same experiment across models to see what improved and what regressed and at what cost; use a stronger or different-provider model as judge to avoid same-model bias, and suppress judge tracing so it doesn't pollute agent traces.
takeaways.numbers: Haiku 5.5: faithfulness 3x better but still bad, more consistent, but 4x cost and defaulted to 'hold' 41/45 times

takeaways.technique: Treat eval prompts as code; XML-tag all data and examples
takeaways.what_they_do: Wrap every input/output/example in XML tags so the judge can distinguish instructions from data; version and test rubric prompts because tiny wording changes flip results; constrain output via tool-call enums rather than string instructions.
takeaways.evidence_quote: I forgot to put XML tags around my examples... when I wrapped them in XML tags, everything suddenly became actionable.
takeaways.numbers: Same data/instructions, only XML tagging changed: results flipped from all 'not actionable' to all 'actionable'
